title: Malaysia continues efforts to find 54 missing in Nepal, says Foreign Minister - The Straits Times
description: Malaysia continues efforts to find 54 missing in Nepal, says Foreign Minister  The Straits Times
publisher.title: The Straits Times
full_article:
KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia is not letting up efforts to trace the 54 missing Malaysians following the Rasuwa disaster in Nepal, after the Nepalese government ended its search-and-rescue operations.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan said the Malaysian Embassy in Kathmandu was working with the local authorities, trekking checkpoints and municipal officials to pursue any remaining leads.

He said information from trekking registration records and the victims’ last known phone signals indicated that most of the missing Malaysians were believed to have been along the route affected by the disaster on Aug 26.

“Although Nepal has ended its search-and-rescue operations and moved into the recovery phase, our embassy is still in contact with trekking posts and the local authorities.

“We will continue trying to locate them for as long as there is still room for us to do so,” he said during the Minister’s Question Time in the Dewan Rakyat on Oct 22.

Mohamad was replying to a question from Member of Parliament Mohd Suhaimi Abdullah on the latest status of Malaysians who remain uncontactable following the disaster in Rasuwa.

He said a total of 5,285 people were still classified as missing, including 636 foreign nationals from 34 countries. Fifty-four of them are Malaysians .

Malaysia had deployed the Special Malaysia Disaster Assistance and Rescue Team to Nepal from Sept 5 to 11 after obtaining approval from the Nepalese authorities, he said.

The team brought nine high-powered drones, but the steep terrain and inaccessible areas limited search efforts.

Mohamad said the Malaysian mission in Kathmandu was continuing to liaise with trekking posts, where hikers are required to register, to establish the movements and last known locations of the missing Malaysians. THE STAR/ASIA NEWS NETWORK

description: 3,585 passengers benefit from free Nepal Police, APF bus services during Dashain  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: A total of 3,585 passengers benefited from free bus services operated by Nepal Police and the Armed Police Force (APF) in the Kathmandu Valley during the Dashain festival.

According to Nepal Police Headquarters, three vehicles operated by Nepal Police provided free transportation to 1,406 passengers on October 20 and 21.

Similarly, APF buses transported 2,179 passengers free of charge over three days beginning October 19, said Shailendra Thapa, deputy spokesperson for the force.

The APF operated two buses in the Kathmandu Valley on Maha Ashtami, Maha Nawami and Bijaya Dashami to help passengers reach their destinations during the festive period.

The free transportation services were introduced to ease travel for the public amid a shortage of public vehicles during Dashain, when many people travel to celebrate the festival with their families.

The initiative helped passengers access transportation during one of Nepal’s busiest festive periods, when increased travel demand often puts pressure on public transport services.

title: Nepal steps up preparations for COP31 climate summit - Khabarhub
description: Nepal steps up preparations for COP31 climate summit  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Nepal has intensified preparations for the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), scheduled to take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20.

According to the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, Nepal’s position paper for the global climate summit is nearing completion. The ministry is collecting feedback and submissions from relevant stakeholders to refine the document before its finalization.

Joint Secretary Dr. Maheshwor Dhakal, chief of the ministry’s Climate Management Division, said the position paper is expected to be unveiled next week. Nepal aims to strengthen its diplomatic efforts at the conference to advance climate justice and secure greater access to international climate finance.

Dhakal emphasized that high-level political representation would be crucial to effectively communicate Nepal’s priorities and concerns at the international forum. While the first week of the conference will focus primarily on technical and thematic negotiations, the second week will feature ministerial-level discussions and decisions on key documents and agreements.

He said the participation of political leaders would be particularly important in negotiations concerning climate finance and adaptation, which are critical for a climate-vulnerable country like Nepal.

The ministry is also working to develop a clear plan for the participation of representatives from federal, provincial and local governments in finalizing the country’s position. However, accommodating the large number of interested participants within limited financial resources remains a challenge.

The recent disaster in Bhotekoshi, which drew international attention to Nepal’s vulnerability to climate-related hazards, is also expected to strengthen the country’s case for greater international support.

Dr. Manish Raj Pandey, director of the Climate Change Department at the National Trust for Nature Conservation, said Nepal should use COP31 to highlight the specific climate risks facing mountain regions, climate-induced loss and damage, and the urgent need for financial support for adaptation.

Pandey stressed that international negotiations should prioritize glacier-lake monitoring, protection of downstream communities exposed to mountain-related disasters, and measures to reduce climate risks.

He also called for adequate funding to address climate-induced loss and damage, rapid assistance to disaster-affected communities, and recognition of non-economic losses, including social and cultural damage.

According to Pandey, climate finance for vulnerable countries should be provided primarily through grants rather than loans to avoid increasing their financial burden. He further emphasized the need to empower local governments and communities to access and effectively use the Adaptation Fund.

He also called for simpler and faster procedures for accessing international climate finance, particularly for national institutions in least developed and mountainous countries.

Climate policy expert Raju Pandit Chhetri highlighted the imbalance in global investment priorities, arguing that conflicts and trade often receive greater attention than climate mitigation and adaptation.

He said COP31 should serve as an opportunity to hold major global powers accountable for increasing climate finance, pointing to the Bhotekoshi floods as an example of the serious risks faced by climate-vulnerable communities.

Climate expert Manjeet Dhakal described COP31 as an important platform for Nepal to draw international attention to its climate risks and vulnerabilities. He stressed that Nepal must fulfil its own emission-reduction commitments while urging developed countries to cut emissions more rapidly and deliver promised climate finance.

Such support, he said, is essential to protecting livelihoods, safeguarding infrastructure and ensuring that climate impacts do not undermine Nepal’s development progress.

title: Deepa Nepali’s 186-day protest goes unheard as government stays silent - The Kathmandu Post
description: Deepa Nepali’s 186-day protest goes unheard as government stays silent  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
On a day when families across Nepal gathered to celebrate Dashain, applying red tika and jamara to their foreheads and receiving blessings from elders, activist Deepa Nepali spent the festival at Kathmandu’s Maitighar Mandala, continuing a protest that has lasted 186 days without a response from the government.

As the country immersed itself in the festive mood, Nepali continued to demand accountability, asking: “How long will caste continue to be placed above human beings?”

She was joined at the protest site on Wednesday by former Constituent Assembly member Binod Pahadi, Dalit rights activist Madan Nepali, Dalit campaigner Sunita Marik, Dalmardan Kami, yoga guru Drishtant Sharma and Ekal Darmali, who expressed solidarity with her campaign.

Nepali said she had been forced to spend the festival on the streets because the state had ignored her demands despite 186 days of protest. Being unable to celebrate a major family festival at home, she said, raised serious questions about caste discrimination, citizens’ dignity and the state’s accountability.

“If a citizen has to stand on the road for 186 days over a fundamental question of humanity, where is the state? Where is the government?” she asked.

Nepali launched the “Government, Is There a Room Vacant?” campaign at Maitighar to demand action against caste-based discrimination, particularly the exclusion of Dalits from rented accommodation. She said the campaign was not directed at any particular landlord or a single incident of housing discrimination, but sought to challenge discriminatory attitudes embedded in society.

Caste discrimination, she said, remained a barrier to social progress. A society that places caste above a person’s humanity reflects a cruel mindset, she added.

Deepa Nepali stages a sit-in at Maitighar Mandala in Kathmandu.

Her protest also draws attention to the persistence of caste discrimination in Nepal’s capital. If people can be denied rented accommodation because of their caste in Kathmandu, the problem raises wider concerns about the experiences of marginalised communities elsewhere in the country.

Nepali said the issue reflected the attitudes and sensitivity of the state and its institutions. She questioned whether those in policy-making positions were willing to confront discrimination.

“I have begun to feel that even those in policy-making positions want to preserve discrimination. Otherwise, why are they silent?” she asked.

Nepali said her campaign was not about supporting or opposing any political party, but about defending the humanity and rights of citizens who had endured injustice and inhumane treatment for years.

She had hoped the government led by Balendra Shah would take concrete steps to address caste discrimination. But the lack of action on her demands over 186 days had left her disillusioned, she said.
